title: Provide instruction to clients and hunting staff

lessons.title: Instructing clients
lessons.html:
Why instruction matters

Many hunting accidents and wounded animals come from poor communication. A professional hunter is a teacher: clients and staff must know exactly what to do, how and why. Good instruction protects lives, the animals and the business's reputation.

Principles of good instruction

  • Know your learner: experience, language, physical fitness, expectations.
  • Explain, demonstrate, practise, check: tell them, show them, let them try, then check they can do it.
  • Keep it simple: short sentences and one point at a time.
  • Be positive and respectful, even when correcting a mistake.
  • Repeat key safety rules often.

What clients need to be instructed on

TopicExamples
Firearm safetyMuzzle control, when to load and unload, safety catch, chamber empty in vehicle
Shooting sticksSetting up quickly and quietly, resting the rifle, steady position
Shot placementHeart-lung area for each species from different angles
Movement in the veldWalk in single file behind the PH, step where the tracker steps, stop at signals
SignalsRaised hand means stop; pointing; "shoot" only on the PH's word
Camp rulesNo alcohol before or during hunting, storage of rifles in the safe
Legal pointsPermit limits, which animals may be shot

Practice before the hunt

Practise on the range from shooting sticks at realistic distances. Use a target showing the animal's outline and vital area. Watch the client's handling and correct unsafe habits immediately and clearly: "Please keep the muzzle pointed down towards the ground while we walk."

lessons.title: Instructing hunting staff
lessons.html:
The hunting team

A hunt depends on trackers, skinners, drivers, camp staff and sometimes apprentice hunters. Each must know their role and how to stay safe.

Daily briefing

Each morning, give a short briefing:

  • Where you will hunt and which species.
  • The role of each person: who tracks, who carries water and the first aid kit, who stays with the vehicle.
  • Radio channels and call signs.
  • Safety points, such as known dangerous animals in the area or a neighbour working near the boundary.
  • Expected return time.

Instructions for trackers

  • Agreed hand signals and how to point out animals silently.
  • Never walk in front of the rifle; stay behind or beside the PH when the client is ready to shoot.
  • Mark the spot of the shot and the last place the animal was seen.
  • How to approach a downed animal safely.

Instructions for skinners and meat handlers

  • Correct skinning cuts for the type of mount the client wants (shoulder mount, full mount, flat skin).
  • Salting and drying skins, and labelling trophies with the client's name and species.
  • Hygiene: clean knives, clean hands, gloves, cool room.
  • Knife safety: always cut away from your body, use a cut-resistant glove, keep knives sharp.
  • Protect against zoonoses such as anthrax: report any animal that died without a clear cause, and never open such a carcass.

Training apprentices

Experienced staff should coach apprentices step by step and let them take responsibility gradually. Give feedback on what went well and what to improve.

Checking understanding

Ask open questions ("What will you do if the animal gets up?") rather than "Do you understand?", which most people answer "yes".

Key points

  • Explain, demonstrate, practise and check.
  • Instruct clients on firearm safety, sticks, shot placement, movement and signals.
  • Correct unsafe habits immediately and respectfully.
  • Brief staff every morning on area, roles, radios and safety.
  • Check understanding with open questions.
